item.title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highly relevant, clear reporting, and impactful story

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

Source: The Guardian Environment | Published: 2026-11-22 13:36 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Plan to breed rare Asian golden cats for pets raises conservation concerns
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail, and conservation focus

An Indonesian company has sought to register a captive-breeding facility with the Secretariat of CITES, the global wildlife trade treaty, to commercially breed and export rare Asian golden cats as pets, report Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman and Fernanda Wenzel.

If approved, PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama would become the first facility in the world to commercially breed Asian golden cats (Catopuma temminckii) in captivity for the international pet market. On behalf of Indonesia, the CITES Secretariat issued a public notification in August, granting signatory countries until Nov. 10 to object before the facility is added to the registry of commercial breeding facilities.

Classified as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, an estimated 7,000 Asian golden cats remain in the wild, threatened by habitat loss, as well as poaching for their skins and bones.

While wild-caught individuals are protected under CITES Appendix I — which bans international commercial trade — captive-bred animals from registered facilities can be legally sold with export permits. According to documents from Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry to the CITES Secretariat, the facility initiated its breeding program in 2013 using four legally acquired wild-caught Asian golden cats. By 2025, the facility reported its population had grown to 36 individuals across three generations.

This rapid reproduction rate and animal welfare standards have come under scrutiny. “They are super challenging to breed,” said Mike Brocklehurst, a carnivore specialist who ran a conservation breeding program for Asian golden cats at Melbourne Zoo in Australia. “A lot of times in captivity, the males kill the female when they’re introduced.”

Brocklehurst said achieving the high breeding rate claimed by Alam Nusantara Jayatama likely relies on hand-rearing kittens pulled early from their mothers, a “speed-breeding” technique that forces females back into estrus sooner.

Sandra Reichler, curator for mammals at Heidelberg Zoo in Germany and head of the European Association of Zoos and Aquariums (EAZA) species breeding program, said early separation causes behavioral deficits and that the company’s 9-square-meter (97-square-feet) enclosures, as shown in photographs, fall far short of EAZA’s recommended 150-m2 (1,615-ft2) minimum. “A commercial breeding centre that only produces golden cats for the private pet market doesn’t help the species in the wild,” Reichler said.

Chris Shepherd, senior conservation advocate at the U.S.-based Center for Biological Diversity, said commercial captive breeding rarely reduces wild demand and often hinders conservation efforts. “The idea that Asian golden cats can be bred in commercial numbers, where profit is actually made … should be investigated. It seems very suspicious,” he said.

Neither Alam Nusantara Jayatama nor owner Danny Gunalen responded to Mongabay’s inquiries by the time the story was published.

Mongabay contacted the CITES Secretariat to confirm whether it has received any objections, but hasn’t received a response. The CITES register of captive breeding facilities does not yet list PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama for Asian golden cats.

Read the full story by Spoorthy Raman and Fernanda Wezel here.

Banner image of an Asian golden cat. Image courtesy of @Zoo Heidelberg.

item.title: Kuala Lumpur otters raise river revival hopes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: positive environmental development, clear reporting

- Smooth-coated otters are increasingly being spotted along Kuala Lumpur’s Klang River, raising hopes that years of cleanup efforts are improving water quality and restoring urban wildlife habitat.

- The otters’ growing presence is not without conflict: habitat loss from development has driven some into residential areas, where they’ve raided fish ponds, prompting calls for residents to adapt rather than harm the protected animals.

- Conservationists and city officials say they hope the otters can galvanize further efforts to clean up the Klang, reduce waste entering the river, and restore more natural riverbanks.

KUALA LUMPUR — Beneath a tangle of highway in the Malaysian capital, a family of otters rolls around in a patch of riverside sand, delighting the few passersby who notice them.

Small groups of otters are now being seen regularly in parts of the city, including along the once heavily polluted Klang River.

Theories vary on whether the smooth-coated otters (Lutrogale perspicillata), classed as vulnerable on the Red List of the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, have returned to the city or were hiding in plain sight all along.

But their presence has raised hopes that efforts to clean up the Klang may be bearing fruit, and could inspire further improvement.

The Klang was once one of the world’s dirtiest waterways, designated a Class 5 severely polluted river under Malaysia’s rankings, the worst possible rating.

Years of work improved it to Class 3, or moderately polluted, which seems to have encouraged the otters to move in, said Malaysian wildlife ecologist Woo Chee Yoong.

“Wherever there are otters, there are fish. Wherever there are fish it means the whole river system [is] clean, it’s healthy for all the communities around. So that’s one of the importance of otters,” he said.

In recent years, the animals have been filmed sunbathing on the river’s concrete banks and swimming in front of elevated metro stations, winning viral fame.

Retired soldier Hasan Ujang, who lives in a riverside apartment, said he enjoys watching their antics.

“We feel really happy when we watch them playing and playing, like kids swimming,” he said.

‘They have to survive’

But unlike otters in neighboring Singapore, which are closely monitored by a network of citizen scientists, little is known about Kuala Lumpur’s otters.

Woo said he learned about them from local media reports on sightings in 2019, and the following year co-founded the Malaysian Otter Network (MON) conservation group.

“We don’t know how many groups are there, we don’t know how actually the otters are moving around,” Woo said.

Even the question of whether the otters have returned to the capital or were simply in less visible city environments before remains a “mystery.”

MON says it hopes to set up a citizen science system for people to report sightings.

Different groups of otters have been spotted elsewhere in the city, including at the Tropicana Golf & Country Resort, a high-end housing estate where they are less welcome visitors.

They are accused of raiding at least 12 houses there in the past year. Their target: fish ponds.

Resident Yee Sze Mun, 89, said otters killed the beloved — and expensive — arowana fish he had nurtured for 15 years.

“They are a nuisance, but I can’t blame them, because they are just like us, they have to survive,” he said.

Residents say the incursions began last year after a company backed by Malaysia’s biggest pension fund, the EPF, began clearing forest next door for Kwasa Damansara, a new township project.

“We have an issue because they’re losing their habitat,” said residents’ association president Joy Appukuttan, who called the otter attacks a “grave concern.”

Alfyan Mohd Adnan, who manages communications for Kwasa Damansara developer, declined to comment.

According to Tropicana’s security team, there are around 25 otters in the forest. The estate has brought in Woo to teach residents how to deal with them.

The species is protected in Malaysia, so Woo urges residents to block entry points to their yards and install fences or netting over ponds.

‘An asset’

Maimunah Mohd Sharif, a former Kuala Lumpur mayor and now adviser to the city on sustainable urbanization, called the otters an “asset.”

“Otters are one of the benchmarks for clean cities,” she said.

Like others, she said she hopes a growing awareness of the Klang River otters can be harnessed to help improve the river further.

Hundreds of garbage traps were installed as part of the government’s River of Life project, and solar-powered “interceptors” deployed by a Dutch NGO have collected tens of thousands of tons of waste.

Now, Maimunah said she wants to see more done to stop waste entering the river in the first place, and efforts to raise the Klang to Class 2B status, clean enough for body contact.

“One day, I want to swim in the Klang River,” she said.

Scarlett Koon Si Qi, a community architect and co-organizer of the annual Klang River Festival, said she hopes the waterway can be restored to its natural banks without concrete lining.

“Some parts, maybe yes, you do need concrete to kind of protect and control for floods,” she said.

“But I think wherever we can, we should leave it as natural as possible.”

That would further benefit the otters, which need some vegetation and natural crevices to hide in, experts said.

The otters are already shifting public views about the river, said Faith Foo, who runs the festival.

Growing up, “the teachers would always say that this is a very unsanitary place,” he said.

But seeing the otters, “it’s a reminder that that is a river.”

Banner image: Smooth-coated otters play on the shore of the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur. Image by Mohd Rasfan / AFP.

This article is part of a reporting project between Mongabay and Agence France-Presse (AFP).
